summary: Adds guidelines for benchmarking IPv6 performance of network interconnect devices such as routers, to be used together with RFC 2544. RFC 2544 is independent of IP version but misses some IPv6 specifics. Transition mechanisms are out of scope. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC adds IPv6-specific details to an existing guide for measuring network-device performance. It tells testers which traffic and conditions to include while keeping the RFC 2544 procedures for other aspects.

subtitle: IPv6-specific test guidance to use alongside the RFC 2544 benchmarking methods

tldr.problem: RFC 2544 gives general methods for benchmarking network devices but does not cover some IPv6 details, such as extension headers and IPv6 address selection.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC adds guidance for test setup, traffic sizes and addresses, extension headers, filters, coexistence tests and the existing RFC 2544 test suite.
tldr.outcome: It complements RFC 2544 rather than replacing it. The back-to-back frames test is not recommended for IPv6, and transition mechanisms are out of scope.

today: RFC 5180 is Informational, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its text says it complements RFC 2544 rather than replacing it.

sections.title: An IPv6 Addendum to RFC 2544
sections.content:
RFC 2544 defines benchmarking methods for network interconnect devices. Its principles are largely independent of IP version, but IPv6 has details that need additional guidance, including extension-header processing. RFC 5180 keeps the RFC 2544 framework and complements its tests and result analysis.

Terms remain consistent with RFC 1242. If this RFC does not address a test-method detail, the RFC 2544 guidance applies. The document notes that not every test applies to every type of network element.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 2544 remains the main test guide. This RFC adds IPv6-specific instructions and directs testers back to RFC 2544 for details it does not cover.

sections.title: Test Setup, Frames and Addresses
sections.content:
The test environment follows RFC 2544 for both single-port and multi-port testing. Neighbor information may be configured manually or learned dynamically; dynamic discovery is preferred when the test tool can keep neighbor caches active. The test traffic should represent endpoints one hop beyond the device under test to avoid neighbor-discovery storms caused by reachability checks.

The RFC gives Ethernet frame sizes of 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 1280 and 1518 bytes, and Packet over SONET sizes of 47, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 1280, 1518, 2048 and 4096 bytes. It reserves 2001:0200::/48 for benchmarking, and says those addresses must not be used as Internet source or destination addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The tests use several packet sizes and a special IPv6 address range set aside for benchmarking. A test tool can configure neighbor details or discover them while the test runs.

sections.title: Testing IPv6 Extension Headers
sections.content:
Benchmark tests should run with no extension headers, with individual extension headers, and with a chain of two or more headers. The recommended chain contains a routing header, a destination-options header and a fragment header; it excludes the hop-by-hop header and ESP.

Every forwarding node must process a hop-by-hop header, so that test measures header-processing effects and device-resource impact rather than ordinary throughput. The RFC calls for testing that traffic at 1%, 10% and 50% of interface bandwidth while monitoring resources. Filters that inspect upper-layer information may also require a device to traverse extension headers.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 packets can carry extra headers between the main header and their data. The tests check packets with these headers, and separately examine the extra work caused by hop-by-hop headers.

sections.title: Modifiers, Performance Tests and Coexistence
sections.content:
The RFC 2544 performance tests remain in use, including throughput, latency, frame loss, system recovery and reset. IPv6 tests should be repeated with different extension-header conditions. Filter tests use IPv6 source and destination addresses and can match IPv6, TCP or UDP traffic, including traffic with extension headers.

Because IPv4 and IPv6 may share a device, the RFC also describes IPv4-only, IPv6-only and mixed-traffic tests. The back-to-back frames test is no longer recommended for IPv6 because its results have significant variance. IPv6 multicast benchmarking is outside this document's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The device is measured for forwarding rate, delay, loss and recovery, with and without filters. The tests also check how IPv4 and IPv6 traffic perform alone and together.

sections.title: Lab Isolation and Conclusion
sections.content:
Benchmarking is intended for a controlled laboratory network using dedicated address space. The test network must not connect to equipment that could forward test traffic into production or misroute it to the management network. Tests treat the device as a black box and should not rely on special benchmarking-only capabilities.

The RFC concludes that RFC 2544 remains applicable to most IPv6 performance testing, with the IPv6-specific requirements in this document used as a complement. IPv6 transition mechanisms are outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Run the tests in an isolated lab so test packets cannot reach a production network. Use RFC 5180 together with RFC 2544, not as a replacement for it.
